fatal_errors: It assumes that fewer constituents necessarily produce less lattice distortion and lower strength. The target results instead show composition-specific MSAD control, with some Cr-containing ternary or quaternary alloys stronger than the quinary alloy.

It omits the dominant temperature-dependent mechanisms: low-temperature inertial dulling caused by reduced phonon drag and high-temperature Portevin–Le Chatelier strengthening from dynamic Mn/Fe solute pinning.
The cited evidence concerns an unrelated BCC Nb-Ta-Ti-V refractory alloy and does not validate the proposed mechanism in FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys.
explanation: The hypothesis partially recovers the central idea that composition-dependent local lattice distortion changes resistance to dislocation glide. It also proposes a controlled compositional series and a falsifiable distortion–strength correlation. However, it incorrectly recasts this as a constituent-count effect with the quinary alloy presumed to have the greatest distortion and strength, contrary to the composition-specific MSAD trend. It does not reconstruct the single-crystal [1̄23] compression program, CRSS measurements over 9–1373 K, strain-rate jumps, thermal-activation fitting, TEM test of Suzuki segregation, or DFT MSAD analysis. Its predictions omit cryogenic CRSS doubling and inertial dulling, as well as high-temperature serrations and Mn+Fe-dependent PL increments. Chemical short-range order and dislocation-core distortion are introduced without relevant supporting evidence. The experiment could test a simplified lattice-distortion hypothesis, but diffraction peak broadening is not by itself a clean measure of static local distortion, and grain, texture, and defect-density effects would need tighter control.
